decomposition-and-refactoring.label: Decomposition and Refactoring
decomposition-and-refactoring.summary: Refactor working code by extracting repeated or separate responsibilities into helper functions while preserving the program's behavior.

sc-refactor-goal.title: What refactoring should preserve
sc-refactor-goal.prompt: What is the main goal when refactoring code that already works?
sc-refactor-goal.hint: The structure may improve, but the program should still do the same job for the same inputs.

help.concept: Refactoring changes code structure without intentionally changing observable behavior.
help.hint_1: Function names and line layout may change.
help.hint_2: The same inputs should still produce the same intended results.

options.a: Improve the structure while preserving the program's behavior
options.b: Change the output so the refactor is easy to notice
options.c: Remove every function from the program
options.d: Keep every original line in exactly the same place

sc-extract-repetition.title: Spot a helper candidate
sc-extract-repetition.prompt: A program uses `name.strip().title()` in four different places. Which refactor best reduces that duplication?
sc-extract-repetition.hint: Move the repeated transformation into one named operation.

help.concept: Repeated logic is a strong candidate for a helper function.
help.hint_1: The cleanup should have one definition.
help.hint_2: Each old duplicate can then be replaced by a helper call.

options.a: Create `clean_name(name)` and call it from each place
options.b: Copy the cleanup into four more places
options.c: Rename all four variables but keep the duplicate cleanup
options.d: Add extra print statements around each copy

sc-one-responsibility.title: Give a helper one clear job
sc-one-responsibility.prompt: Which helper has the clearest single responsibility in a program that reads text, counts words, and formats a report?
sc-one-responsibility.hint: A helper is easiest to understand when its name describes one focused task.

help.concept: Decomposition separates distinct jobs so each function has a clear responsibility.
help.hint_1: Counting words is one focused transformation.
help.hint_2: Reading input, counting, formatting, and printing all at once mixes several responsibilities.

options.b: `do_everything()` reads input, counts, formats, and prints

sc-helper-reuse.title: Reuse an existing helper
sc-helper-reuse.prompt: `clean_name(name)` already returns a cleaned name. Inside `build_badge(name)`, which line best reuses that existing responsibility?
sc-helper-reuse.hint: Call the helper instead of rewriting its `.strip().title()` logic.

help.concept: Once a responsibility has a helper, other functions should call that helper instead of duplicating its implementation.
help.hint_2: Store or use the value returned by `clean_name(name)`.

try-decomposition-and-refactoring-sketch.title: Refactor repeated name cleanup
try-decomposition-and-refactoring-sketch.prompt: This program already produces the correct output, but it repeats whitespace trimming followed by title-case normalization for both names. Refactor it without changing the output: define `clean_name(name)` so it returns the cleaned name, then replace both repeated cleanup expressions with calls to `clean_name`.
try-decomposition-and-refactoring-sketch.hint: The finished program should still print the same two cleaned names; only the structure changes.

help.concept: A refactor can preserve output while moving repeated logic into one reusable helper.
help.hint_2: Use `clean_name(first)` and `clean_name(second)` instead of repeating the method chain.

try-decomposition-and-refactoring-sketch.starterCode:
first = input()
second = input()

first_clean = first.strip().title()
second_clean = second.strip().title()

print(first_clean)
print(second_clean)
try-decomposition-and-refactoring-sketch.solutionCode:
def clean_name(name):
    return name.strip().title()

first = input()
second = input()

first_clean = clean_name(first)
second_clean = clean_name(second)

print(first_clean)
print(second_clean)

extract-repetition.title: Extract repeated work into one helper
extract-repetition.bodyMarkdown:
**Refactoring** improves the structure of working code without intentionally changing what the program does.

Suppose this program already works:

```python
first = "  ava  "
second = "  mia  "

print(first.strip().title())
print(second.strip().title())
```

The cleanup rule is repeated. A refactor can give that responsibility one name:

```python
def clean_name(name):
    return name.strip().title()

first = "  ava  "
second = "  mia  "

print(clean_name(first))
print(clean_name(second))
```

Both versions produce the same output. The second version is easier to change because the cleanup rule lives in one place.

extract-responsibility.title: Move one responsibility out of the main flow
extract-responsibility.bodyMarkdown:
Decomposition is not only about repeated code. A block can also become clearer when one distinct job gets its own helper.

Before refactoring:

```python
text = "one two three"
words = text.split()
count = len(words)
print(f"Words: {count}")
```

After extracting the counting responsibility:

```python
def count_words(text):
    return len(text.split())

text = "one two three"
count = count_words(text)
print(f"Words: {count}")
```

`count_words` now has one clear job: produce a word count. The main flow still decides how that count is displayed.
